case_study.headline: Some interfaces can’t afford to be confusing
case_study.lead: I designed a custom SOP app for a T-cell cancer therapy lab. It’s built around how technicians actually work, not a generic template.

tldr.title: The next required action, obvious at a glance
tldr.body:
Clear step sequencing and a strong visual hierarchy make the next required action obvious at a glance. The result was 86% fewer procedural errors and 78% faster onboarding.

The app, ACTA SOP, covers the full life of a lab procedure on a tablet: building a standard operating procedure, running it as an experiment, recording data and quality checks, and sending the finished report for signature.

stats.label: guided stages, from experiment details to signature

sections.label: Ideation
sections.title: Starting with the structure of an SOP
sections.intro: I used low-fidelity wireframes to settle how an SOP is built before moving to visual design.

items.heading: A contents rail and step blocks
items.body: A contents rail on the left lists every stage of the SOP: define parameters, materials, procedure overview, quality control and the report builder. Each step is a block with its own details and definition, and form controls are dragged in from a side panel.
items.caption: Wireframes for creating a new SOP.

sections.label: Designs
sections.title: Built for the lab bench
sections.intro:
ACTA SOP is designed for tablets. Each screen puts status first and the next action within reach.

Experiments appear as cards with code, title, owner and date. A colour-coded status (draft, pending or completed) repeats as a bar along the card edge, so where things stand reads before any text does.

items.heading: A dashboard that counts what needs attention
items.body: The dashboard opens with four counts: experiments approved, in review, awaiting approval and needing rework. Filters narrow it to the last 7, 15 or 30 days, and a table below lists each experiment with its owner, role, status and progress.
items.caption: Dashboard with status counts and an experiments table.

items.heading: A sortable SOP library
items.body: Custom SOPs live in a table of code, title, owner, status and category. A filter and sorting panel, pagination and a persistent Create New SOP button keep the library easy to scan and easy to add to.
items.caption: Custom SOP list with the filters and sorting panel open.

items.heading: Signing off with a clear trail
items.body: Signature Progress shows reviewers and approvers in sequence. Each reviewer’s signed ID, date, time and comment sit beside a progress bar (2 of 4 reviewed), so anyone can see who has signed and who is still to come.
items.caption: Signature progress for reviewers and approvers.

sections.label: System
sections.title: One set of components
sections.intro: Filters and sorting, a calendar date picker, a rich-text toolbar, experiment cards and a navigation rail with an icon for each stage share one visual language.

items.caption: Filters, date picker, text toolbar, experiment cards and navigation icons.

case_study.headline: Making financial data easier to understand
case_study.lead: I redesigned key parts of a financial dashboard to improve transaction visibility, simplify navigation, and help users understand their finances faster during everyday workflows.

tldr.title: Hiding complexity is the whole job
tldr.body:
Burq is Folio3's low-code integration platform. It connects eCommerce stores like Amazon and Magento to ERPs like Dynamics 365, so orders, inventory and billing stay in sync. The complexity underneath never goes away; it has to be hidden well.

As Lead Product Designer, I redesigned the whole product. I reshaped the UI and simplified the UX and motion, so the complexity stopped leaking into the user's experience. I also led the design of the ERP integration features, the highest-stakes part of the product. A confusing integration flow doesn't just frustrate people; it breaks their downstream workflows.

impact.title: The Impact
impact.intro: The redesign helped the team move faster and handle more, without adding headcount.

sections.label: Problem
sections.title: Powerful under the hood, confusing on the surface
sections.intro:
Burq could move data between almost any store and any ERP, but the old dashboard didn't tell users what was going on. It led with a chart of errors, gave a third of the screen to a list of integrations, and left key panels as empty placeholders.

How can we make a complex integration platform feel calm enough that teams trust it with their order-to-cash flow?

items.caption: Before: the original dashboard

sections.label: Research
sections.title: Looking past the integrations
sections.intro: I reviewed the existing product with the engineering team and spoke with project developer and finance users to check the integrations and the connectors. I wanted to understand where people got stuck and what they actually checked each day.

items.heading: Key insights
items.body:
**Setup was the biggest drop-off.** Connecting a store to an ERP meant mapping fields across two systems at once, and many users needed support to finish.

**Failures surfaced too late.** A failed order sync often showed up days later, as a mismatch in the ERP or a missing invoice.

**Users think in orders, not API calls.** Ops and finance teams track orders, stock and revenue, but the old dashboard led with technical logs.

sections.label: Ideation
sections.title: Rethinking the hierarchy first
sections.intro: Before touching visuals, I mapped what each user needed to see first. Status and actions moved to the top; logs and settings moved a level down.

items.heading: Testing interaction flows early
items.body: I prototyped the integration setup and error-recovery flows in low fidelity and walked through them with engineers early. That surfaced edge cases, like partial syncs and expired credentials, before the high-fidelity work began.
items.caption: Early flows for connecting apps and recovering from failed syncs.

sections.label: Designs
sections.title: Rebuilding the dashboard from the ground up
sections.intro: Make every screen lead with what matters, and let motion explain rather than decorate. Across 55+ views, the dashboard was rebuilt around one rule: the most important action is never buried.

items.caption: After: the redesigned home dashboard

items.heading: User sees what needs attention first
items.body: The dashboard opens on orders synced, revenue processed and integrations that need action. The user switches between day, week, month and quarter to spot trends, and status colours flag problems before they reach the ERP.
items.caption: Home dashboard focused on workspaces, transaction status and connection health.

items.heading: User connects their apps in a few guided steps
items.body: The user picks a store and an ERP from the integrations marketplace and authenticates both in one flow. Burq suggests field mappings, so the user reviews them instead of building from scratch.
items.caption: ERP integration flow, allowing setup without technical help.

items.heading: User fixes failed syncs in place
items.body: A failed sync shows which order failed, why, and what to do next, in plain language. The user corrects it and retries without leaving the screen. Subtle motion confirms each step, so the user always knows the system responded.
items.caption: Error recovery with purposeful micro-interactions.

sections.label: Lessons
sections.title: Designing for calm, clarity and confidence in complex workflows

items.heading: Key takeaways
items.body:
**Simplify, don't strip.** I didn't remove motion; I gave it a job. Purposeful micro-interactions made the product feel faster and more trustworthy than a static UI would.

**Design for the person, not the system.** I started out designing around how integrations worked. The real gains came from designing around how ops and finance teams work: in orders, stock and cash.

quote.text: Consistently translated complex requirements into clean, intuitive, and visually engaging interfaces.
quote.author: Hussain Imtiaz Ali

case_study.headline: A handbook that makes the case for Sharjah at a glance
case_study.lead: I designed the Investor Handbook for Invest in Sharjah, the emirate’s investment promotion agency, for Expo 2020 Dubai: a print publication that turns economic data, sector profiles and the agency’s services into clear, scannable spreads.

case_study.headline: One brand, from billboard to back office
case_study.lead: I designed Propertico's brand, its off-plan property website and the dashboard its team uses to run maintenance. Maintenance tasks now get resolved 75% faster.
case_study.categories: Brand Identity, Website, Property Management Dashboard

tldr.title: Two very different users, each feeling it was built for them
tldr.body:
Propertico is KV Group's Dubai property company. It helps people buy off-plan homes as first homes or investments, then manages those homes once landlords and tenants move in. Buyers need confidence and clear numbers; the operations team needs speed and a clear schedule. I designed both sides.

First the brand: the logo, colours, stationery, signage and billboards. Then the website and 16+ campaigns that bring buyers in. Then the property management dashboard the operations team uses to schedule check-ins, cleaning and repairs. I mapped the full journey for both sides before a single high-fidelity screen was built, and that groundwork made everything after it faster and more consistent.

impact.title: The Impact
impact.intro: One consistent brand outside, and a calmer operation inside.

sections.label: Problem
sections.title: Selling a dream, then keeping it running
sections.intro:
Propertico had two jobs that pull in opposite directions. Selling off-plan homes takes a brand that feels premium and trustworthy, because buyers pay for something that isn't built yet.

Running homes after handover takes a fast, plain tool, because a leak at 10am can't wait for a meeting.

items.caption: Before: the original dashboard

sections.label: Research
sections.title: Listening to both sides
sections.intro: I spoke with sales and the operations team, went through enquiries and maintenance logs, and sat with the maintenance coordinators to see how they planned a day. I wanted to know what made a buyer trust an off-plan home, and where maintenance jobs got stuck.

items.heading: Key insights
items.body:
**Buyers trust numbers before pictures.** Investors wanted the price per sq ft, the expected return and the handover date before they cared about the render.

**Coordinators think in days and units, not tickets.** They plan the week by time slot and apartment, so a calendar made more sense to them than a list.

**Not every job is equal.** An urgent AC repair and a routine inspection looked the same in a chat thread. Priority had to be visible at a glance.

sections.label: Ideation
sections.title: Starting with the brand and the journey
sections.intro: I mapped the full journey for both sides first: from a buyer seeing an ad to enquiring, and from a request coming in to a job marked done. That showed where each audience needed confidence and where it needed speed.

items.heading: A mark built on home and connection
items.body: The logo is a roof inside an open arch: a home, held by the people around it. Deep teal and warm cream carry it across business cards, signage, mugs and billboards, with a yellow highlight for key words. The line "Discover your perfect address. Creating connections that last forever." set the tone for everything after.
items.caption: Logo mark and brand colours.

items.heading: Building the system before the screens
items.body: I built a Figma design system with Auto Layout, Variables, Variants and Design Tokens. It grew to 40+ reusable components, so new screens were assembled, not drawn from scratch. I used v0.dev and Lovable to try layout options quickly, then took the strongest into Figma.
items.caption: Dashboard components built on the design system.

sections.label: Designs
sections.title: Premium where buyers look, plain where the team works
sections.intro: The outside sells a dream; the inside keeps it running. The website and campaigns lead with the numbers investors trust. The dashboard leads with today's tasks, their priority and who is on them.

items.caption: After: the redesigned home dashboard

items.heading: Buyer sees the numbers that matter first
items.body: The website opens on "Buy the Dream Before It's Built" and goes straight to Dubai's market highlights. Buyers search on a map by location, developer or project. Each property shows its price, price per sq ft, expected return and handover date side by side.
items.caption: Website hero, map search and property details.

items.heading: Campaigns that teach while they sell
items.body: I designed 16+ campaigns and social creatives in the same brand. The Buy.Propertico posts answer real buyer questions, like why two identical homes cost different amounts, and point to guides on Dubai's top returns.
items.caption: Buy.Propertico social posts.

items.heading: Coordinator sees the whole day at a glance
items.body: The dashboard opens on five counts: active tasks, pending requests, check-ins and check-outs, urgent queries and team on duty. Below, a weekly calendar shows every job by time and unit, and Today's Requests lists jobs by priority with their assignee.
items.caption: Maintenance coordinator screen.

items.heading: Coordinator creates and assigns a task in one panel
items.body: From the Maintenance Requests board, the coordinator opens Add New Task in a side panel. They pick the property, task type, staff member and priority, add notes and create it, without losing sight of the board.
items.caption: Maintenance Requests board with the Add New Task panel.

items.heading: Every task has one source of truth
items.body: Task Details shows status, assignee, priority, schedule, full address and notes in one place, with the assignee's details beside it. Update, Reschedule and Reassign sit at the bottom, so a change takes one click, not a phone call. This is where the 75% faster resolution came from.
items.caption: Task details with assignee information.

sections.label: Lessons
sections.title: Designing for both sides of the door

items.heading: Key takeaways
items.body:
**Map the whole journey first.** Mapping both sides before high fidelity felt slow at the start. It made every later screen faster to design and more consistent to build.

**Different users need different tones.** Buyers needed polish and confidence; coordinators needed plain, fast screens. One design system of 40+ components let both feel built for them.

**Status is a feature.** The biggest gain for the operations team wasn't a new screen; it was always knowing where each task stood and who owned it.

case_study.headline: Thoughtful design belongs in public infrastructure too
case_study.lead: People don’t use government platforms because they like the brand. They use them because they have to. For ADGPG, Abu Dhabi’s government procurement platform, I designed core inner-page modules within the TAMM design system, giving them the same care as any consumer product.

tldr.title: Procurement as a guided process, not paperwork
tldr.body:
I designed 54+ modules that feel native to TAMM. Procurement now works less like paperwork and more like a guided process, with clear steps and clear status. The result was 86% faster processing and a 75% improvement in task completion.

The portal serves two audiences, suppliers and government employees. The homepage welcomes both and routes each to the right content through two clear entry points, followed by cards for government tenders and supplier guidance.

sections.label: Structure
sections.title: Mapping how the pages fit together
sections.intro: I mapped the platform as a sitemap: a top-level page branching into content areas, listing pages, detail pages and forms, colour-coded by type so the whole structure can be read in one view.

items.caption: Sitemap of the platform’s page types and how they connect.

sections.label: Designs
sections.title: Clear steps, clear status
sections.intro: The modules are built on a shared set of cards, tabs, filters and search so that every part of the portal behaves the same way, and a supplier or government employee always knows where to go next.

items.heading: Search that suggests as you type
items.body: The resource library opens with a search bar, popular shortcuts (review contracts, register as a supplier, learn about the new roles) and filters by audience: end user, legal, finance and procurement employee. As the user types, suggestions such as "Award a contract to entities" appear. Each card offers a Read Article link and, where there is one, a downloadable resource.
items.caption: Resource library with search suggestions.

items.heading: Do’s and don’ts and tenders in one place
items.body: Tabs switch between the Do’s & Don’ts for suppliers and tender content, with search, a filter and a card grid below. The highlighted card shows both actions together: Read Article and Downloadable Resource.
items.caption: Tabbed guidance with search and filter.

items.heading: About ADGPG at a glance
items.body: A summary band presents key figures (initiatives launched, entities onboarded, number of tenders and number of suppliers) beside a short introduction to ADGPG. Below it, a News & Announcements carousel keeps updates close.
items.caption: About ADGPG with key figures and news.

case_study.headline: A brand built around growth and momentum
case_study.lead: I redesigned the Go4Trades brand and carried it across its website, print, social media and promotions: a new logo, a navy and mint palette and one consistent voice for a proprietary trading firm.

tldr.title: One identity, from logo to campaigns
tldr.body:
The identity centres on a new logo that fuses the number 4 with an upward-moving arrow, set in a dark navy and mint palette with soft gradient glows. I applied it to the website, business cards, brochures, merchandise, social posts and promotional campaigns, including Arabic versions.

The line Where dreams meet reality runs through the brand.

sections.label: Logo
sections.title: A 4 that points up
sections.intro: The previous logo set a red 4 with an arrow beside the name. The new mark is a single mint ribbon that forms both a 4 and an upward-moving arrow, symbolising growth, momentum and success in the financial markets. It represents the journey of traders striving for higher performance, and the brand’s commitment to opportunity, progress and excellence in proprietary trading.

items.caption: Before and after: the Go4Trades logo.

sections.label: Brand
sections.title: The mark, applied everywhere
sections.intro: The mark and the navy and mint palette carry onto merchandise and stationery: a shirt, cap, tote bag, coffee cup, badges, a billboard and business cards that carry the line Where dreams meet reality.

items.caption: Brand applications: apparel, billboard, cup, cards and badges.

items.heading: Print and offers
items.body: Printed pieces keep the same look: business cards with a QR code, a $50 voucher with a promo code, and a tri-fold brochure whose cover asks Don’t take the risk! Inside, a Why We’re the Real Deal panel sets out the benefits, and a page introduces the KHDA-certified academy.
items.caption: Business card, voucher and tri-fold brochure.

sections.label: Website
sections.title: A dark, glowing interface for traders
sections.intro: The website carries the identity into a dark navy interface with glowing gradients and 3D illustrations. The hero asks A Place Where Dreams Meet Reality. Inner pages explain the firm and its scaling plan, and a set of trading calculators lets visitors work through earnings, profit and loss, and risk.

items.caption: Trading calculators, About and Scaling Plan pages.

sections.label: Social
sections.title: Campaigns for every channel
sections.intro: Social and community content reuses the mark and palette, with an astronaut motif for the community campaigns.

items.heading: Social posts
items.body: Instagram posts announce the new website, share a message about preparation over emotion in trading, and highlight the TradingView-powered charts.
items.caption: Instagram posts.

items.heading: Discord community
items.body: A Rise to the Challenge campaign for Discord uses an astronaut character in a dark green scene, with matching avatars, a banner and a $30 giveaway.
items.caption: Discord campaign graphics and avatars.

items.heading: Offers and promotions
items.body: Graphics for challenge discounts and a flash sale come in English and Arabic versions. They share one layout system of mint headlines, a promo code and coin and planet imagery.
items.caption: Promotional graphics in English and Arabic.

case_study.headline: An AI companion that plans your day at the Forum
case_study.lead: I designed a mobile app that helps delegates plan their day at the World Economic Forum. An AI planner builds an itinerary around their interests and available time, accounts for walking between venues, and flags conflicts before they happen.

tldr.title: From an empty schedule to a plan in five steps
tldr.body:
The app turns planning into a short flow: ask the AI planner, declare interests, read the plan, adjust a slot if there is a conflict, and confirm. Live updates for room changes and cancellations keep the plan current.

The interface stays light and calm, with soft blue gradients, dark session cards for emphasis and a floating tab bar.

sections.label: Flow
sections.title: Five steps from question to itinerary
sections.intro: The core journey has five steps: Ask AI, Declare interests, Read the plan, Adjust slot, and Confirm and go.

items.caption: Steps 1 to 3: ask the AI planner, declare interests and read the plan.
Steps 4 and 5: adjust a slot and confirm the itinerary.

sections.label: Designs
sections.title: A day at a glance
sections.intro: The app opens on a greeting and a single prompt, Let’s plan your schedule, with today’s sessions beneath it.

items.heading: Interests in, itinerary out
items.body: Delegates pick focus areas such as food systems, AI and technology, finance and markets or climate. The AI-generated itinerary then lists recommended sessions with their time, hall and duration, and adds the walking time between venues, even leaving time for a coffee.
items.caption: Choosing interests and the AI-generated itinerary.

items.heading: A home screen that stays current
items.body: The home screen shows the afternoon plan, a search for sessions, speakers and venues, and live updates such as a room change or a cancelled roundtable.
items.caption: Home with the afternoon plan and live updates.

items.heading: Planning, conflicts and sign-in
items.body: The sign-in screen invites delegates to navigate the Forum with an AI companion by their side. A slider sets the time available, for example 2h 30m this afternoon from 14:00 to 16:30. If a session overlaps another commitment, the app detects the conflict and offers two options: keep the current plan and skip one session, or let AI suggest a replacement that fits their interests.
items.caption: Sign-in, home, available time and conflict resolution.

case_study.headline: Making trust visible in every pixel
case_study.lead: Buna moves money across borders for banks and financial institutions. Its whole offer depends on trust. I designed the website so that every layout, tone and hierarchy choice signals security and credibility before a visitor reads a word.

tldr.body:
Across 24+ pages, I balanced scale and reliability with warmth, and explained cross-border payments in a way anyone could follow. The result was a 72% increase in qualified institutional leads.

The site covers who Buna is, its capabilities, its network, news and events, resources, a developer portal and careers, all under one green, gold and white identity.

sections.label: Homepage
sections.title: A hero that explains Buna in five steps
sections.intro: The first screen has to build trust fast. The hero rotates through five messages (Introduction, Cost-Efficient, Secure, Global Standard and Announcement), each with its own illustration and colour, tracked by a numbered progress line along the bottom.

items.caption: Hero slide introducing smooth and efficient onboarding.

sections.label: Pages
sections.title: A system for the inner pages
sections.intro: Inner pages follow a few repeatable patterns so a large site stays easy to scan: a green gradient header with the main navigation, a breadcrumb, a bold title, short intro text and a supporting visual, followed by full-width bands for the detail.

items.heading: Explaining the network at a glance
items.body: The Strategic Objectives & Business Approach page uses a diagram to show Buna at the centre of banks in different countries, so the cross-border idea is clear before the text is read. Compliance Program and a Business Impacts and Tangible Value section with icons follow the same pattern.
items.caption: Compliance Program, homepage and Strategic Objectives & Business Approach.

items.heading: A Careers page for banks
items.body: The Careers section includes a page called How We Hire Banks. Long-form text sits beside a supporting photograph, and a green How We Work band leads into the next section.
items.caption: How We Hire Banks, with placeholder text.

sections.label: Brand
sections.title: Values in one glance
sections.intro: The Our Values section presents Integrity, Reliability, Accountability, Commitment and Excellence on a solid green band, each with a white line icon, a gold title and a one-sentence description.

items.caption: Our Values.

case_study.headline: Making expense claims quick to file and easy to track
case_study.lead: I designed a mobile expense app for Folio3 where employees submit reimbursement requests, scan receipts and follow each claim through to payment, with a separate flow for the finance team that manages the setup.
case_study.categories: Product Design, Mobile App, Expense Management

tldr.title: I manage people, not expenses
tldr.body:
The app’s promise is in its sign-in line: I manage people, not expenses. Employees sign in with Google, see what is due on the home screen, file a request in a few steps and track it to payment. Finance admins manage employees, approvers, locations, designations, roles and expense types.

I mapped the flows for both roles and wireframed the employee view, then moved into the final interface.

sections.label: Structure
sections.title: Two roles, two flows
sections.intro: I mapped user flows for the Employee and the Admin (Finance) roles. Both start with a Google sign-in. A new user is sent on to complete a short profile with employee ID, contact, location, designation and bank account number.

items.caption: User flows for the employee and the finance admin.

items.heading: Wireframing the employee view
items.body: Low-fidelity wireframes covered the login and dashboard screens, the profile screens and a multi-screen New Request flow, including the calendar and the receipt upload steps.
items.caption: Employee view wireframes.

sections.label: Designs
sections.title: The deadline, the requests and the next action
sections.intro: The home screen leads with a deadline banner (for example, 12 days remaining to submit allowable expenses), followed by the employee’s recent and pending requests. A bottom bar holds Home, a red New Request button and My Profile. The banner comes in blue and red variants.

items.heading: One style from sign-in to confirmation
items.body: From the sign-in screen to the "request submitted" confirmation, the screens share one blue and white style, with a single red action reserved for starting a new request.
items.caption: Sign-in, home, reimbursement form, filters and confirmation.

items.heading: Scan receipts, then confirm the details
items.body: Employees photograph receipts, review each scanned item (date incurred and amount in PKR) with an Add more option, then complete a Reimbursement Form with expense type, division and a description before submitting. The form shows the uploaded receipts as thumbnails.
items.caption: Scanning receipts and completing the reimbursement form.

items.heading: Tracking and filtering requests
items.body: My Request lists each claim with its amount and a status tag: Pending, Amount Disbursed or Posted to payroll. A filter sheet narrows the list by expense type, status and date, including a custom date range calendar.
items.caption: Request list, custom date range and filters.

items.heading: Profile and notifications
items.body: Employees can view and edit their profile (employee ID, email, role, bank account, designation, contact and location), and a notifications list reminds them of upcoming deadlines.
items.caption: Profile, edit profile and notifications.
